Last month I reviewed a codebase where 70% was AI-generated.

What I found kept me up at night.

The code was clean. Well-structured. Good variable names.
It was also riddled with:

→ SQL concatenation instead of parameterized queries
→ User input passed directly to shell commands
→ JWT tokens stored in localStorage
→ CORS set to wildcard
→ Hardcoded API keys (yes, in 2026)

The developer wasn't careless. They were fast.
The AI wasn't malicious. It was trained on insecure code.

25.7% of AI-generated code contains at least one vulnerability.
14% ships with leaked secrets or hardcoded credentials.

AI makes you code faster.
It doesn't make you code safer.

Human review is now more important, not less.

-Nish

The patch window is dead.

Mandiant's 2026 data shows the average time-to-exploit has gone negative.

-7 days.

That means exploitation is landing roughly a week BEFORE a fix is available.

For remote access infrastructure? 10 hours from disclosure to exploit.

The old model:
→ CVE published
→ You assess impact
→ You schedule patching
→ You deploy

The new reality:
→ Exploitation begins
→ CVE published (maybe)
→ You find out you're affected
→ Damage already done

90 zero-days were exploited in the wild in 2025. 48% targeted enterprise infrastructure.

You don't have time to figure out what you have when the CVE drops.

You need to know before.

Continuous vulnerability assessment → zerosight360.com

Security reviews feel like a lecture from someone who's never shipped code.

I get it.

What developers hear:
→ "Slow down."
→ "Add more steps."
→ "You're doing it wrong."

What we actually mean:
→ "Ship faster."
→ "Without the 3am incident call."
→ "Let's make secure the easy path."

The friction isn't the security review.
It's the timing.

Finding issues in production = firefighting.
Finding issues in PR review = 5-minute fix.
Finding issues in design = free.

Security that shows up at the end is always a blocker.
Security that shows up at the start is a shortcut.

We're not here to slow you down.
We're here to keep you from getting slowed down later.

-Nish

52% of API breaches come from one thing.

Broken authentication.

Not sophisticated attacks. Not zero-days.
Just... endpoints that don't properly verify who's calling them.

Worse: 59% of API vulnerabilities require no authentication at all.

The pattern we see over and over:

→ API built for internal use
→ Later exposed to partners
→ Later exposed to mobile app
→ Authentication "added later"
→ Inconsistently applied
→ Breach

Your API count is growing faster than your team can track.

5,900+ APIs per enterprise on average.
258 attacks per organization last year.
$700K average cost per incident.

Every endpoint is an attack surface.
Do you know where yours are?

API security assessment → zerosight360.com

They had 18 months of runway.

A single breach cut it to 3.

Series A startup. 40 employees. Growing fast.
Security was "on the roadmap" — right after the next funding round.

Then:
→ Customer data exfiltrated
→ Mandatory disclosure to affected users
→ Enterprise prospects froze their deals
→ Insurance claim denied (no MFA requirement met)
→ Legal fees started piling up

$4M+ in direct and indirect costs.

The breach didn't kill them.
The trust damage did.

Their biggest enterprise prospect — the one that would've changed everything — walked.

"We can't onboard a vendor with an active breach investigation."

I'm not here to fear-monger.

I'm here because I've seen this story too many times.

Security isn't a cost center.
It's runway insurance.

-Nish

Most security checklists are compliance theater.

Here's what actually prevents breaches:

✓ Threat modeling BEFORE code
Not after. Not during pentest. Before the first line.

✓ SAST in every PR
Not weekly scans. Every pull request. Developers fix while context is fresh.

✓ Dependency scanning on merge
86% of codebases have vulnerable dependencies. Catch them before they ship.

✓ Secret detection pre-commit
14% of AI-generated projects ship with leaked credentials. Block them locally.

✓ DAST in staging
Catch what static analysis misses. Every deployment.

✓ Continuous pentesting
Annual tests made sense when exploit windows were 63 days. They're now -7 days.

The pattern: shift left, automate, make secure the default.

68% of breaches involve a human element.
Reduce the decisions humans have to make.

Secure SDLC implementation → zerosight360.com

True story: I found a Fortune 500's customer database in 20 minutes.

No hacking required. I just... looked.

The bucket was set to public during "quick testing" three years ago.
It was supposed to be temporary.

They had:
→ Expensive security tools
→ Annual penetration tests
→ SOC 2 Type II certification
→ A dedicated security team

But this bucket was created outside the normal process.
A developer needed something fast for a demo.
It worked. They moved on.

Three years and 2.3 million customer records later, I found it during a routine assessment.

19.6 billion files are exposed in misconfigured cloud buckets right now.
685,000 credential files. Sitting open.

The gap isn't technology.
It's visibility.

What exists outside your official infrastructure?

-Nish

23% of cloud breaches start with one checkbox.

Not sophisticated attacks.
Not insider threats.
Not zero-days.

Misconfiguration.

The numbers:
→ 3,000+ misconfigured cloud assets per enterprise at any given time
→ 180 days average detection time for config issues
→ 37% YoY increase in cloud-conscious intrusions

The pattern:
→ Developer creates resource for testing
→ Sets it to public "temporarily"
→ Forgets about it
→ Moves on to next project
→ Resource stays public for months/years

"An S3 bucket made public at 2pm can be discovered and downloaded by 2:30pm."

Automated scanners run 24/7 looking for exactly this.

Your cloud provider gives you infinite flexibility.
It also gives you infinite rope.

Cloud security assessment → zerosight360.com

I found an IAM policy that said:

{
  "Action": "*",
  "Resource": "*",
  "Effect": "Allow"
}

Created by a senior engineer.
In production for 2 years.

No one reviewed it.
No one questioned it.
It just... worked.

Until it didn't.

The senior engineer wasn't negligent. They were solving a problem at 2am during an outage. The broad permissions fixed the immediate issue. The TODO to tighten them never got done.

We found this in a routine assessment.

Every organization has these. The temporary fixes that became permanent. The shortcuts that never got cleaned up.

I'm not here to blame the engineer.
I'm here to find these before someone else does.

-Nish

Your containers are secure.

Your container images aren't.

The supply chain problem nobody talks about:

→ Base image: 47 CVEs (3 critical)
→ OS packages: Outdated, unpatched
→ App dependencies: 23 critical vulns at level 8
→ Your code: Scanned, clean
→ Runtime: Unmonitored

You scan your code religiously.
But your code is only one layer.

The image it runs on? Inherited vulnerabilities.
The packages it depends on? 911 components on average.
The runtime it executes in? Often invisible to security tools.

4 layers. 3 blind spots. 1 compromised container.

Container security isn't just scanning your Dockerfile.
It's the entire supply chain from base image to runtime.

Container security assessment → zerosight360.com

"It's in a private VPC. It's secure."

I hear this weekly.

Private VPC. Public S3 endpoint.
Private VPC. NAT gateway to internet.
Private VPC. Overly permissive security groups.
Private VPC. IAM role with admin access.

The VPC being "private" doesn't mean:
→ Your data can't leave it
→ Your services can't be misconfigured
→ Your IAM policies are correct
→ Your endpoints are authenticated

It means your EC2 instances don't have public IPs.

That's it.

The perimeter isn't the VPC boundary anymore.
It's every service, every endpoint, every identity.

Private network ≠ private data.

-Nish

Where does your cloud security actually stand?

Level 1 - Reactive
→ No inventory. Alert fatigue. Fighting fires.

Level 2 - Aware
→ Basic scanning. Some policies. Inconsistent enforcement.

Level 3 - Defined
→ Standards documented. Guardrails in place. Still manual.

Level 4 - Managed
→ Automated enforcement. Continuous monitoring. Metrics tracked.

Level 5 - Optimized
→ Security as code. Predictive detection. Continuous improvement.

Most organizations think they're at Level 3.
Most are actually at Level 2.

The gap: documentation vs enforcement.

Having a policy doesn't mean it's followed.
Having a tool doesn't mean it's configured correctly.
Having a process doesn't mean it scales.

Honest assessment is the first step.

Cloud security maturity assessment → zerosight360.com

Unpopular opinion:

AI isn't making security harder.
It's exposing how bad we already were.

The vulnerabilities AI introduces? We were writing those manually.
The phishing emails AI generates? We were falling for worse.
The malware AI creates? Script kiddies had templates.

AI just made all of it:
→ Faster
→ Cheaper
→ More scalable

The tools changed.
The failures didn't.

We're not losing to AI.
We're losing to the same problems we always had:
→ Too many alerts, not enough context
→ Too much surface area, not enough visibility
→ Too many tools, not enough integration

AI amplifies everything.
Including our existing gaps.

-Nish

Your employees are using AI tools you don't know about.

$670,000

That's what shadow AI adds to breach costs per incident.

20% of all breaches now involve unauthorized AI tools.

The pattern:
→ Employee signs up for AI tool with work email
→ Pastes code/data into prompts
→ AI trains on or stores that data
→ Data surfaces in other users' outputs
→ You find out during incident response

The tools aren't malicious.
The usage isn't authorized.
The data isn't protected.

You can't secure what you can't see.

Blocking isn't the answer — they'll find workarounds.
Visibility is. Policy is. Training is.

What AI tools are your employees using?
What data are they sharing?

AI security assessment → zerosight360.com

I gave 10 AI coding assistants the same 50 prompts.

The results were... educational.

Vulnerable code generated:
→ GPT-4o: 62%
→ Claude 3: 58%
→ GitHub Copilot: 55%
→ Gemini: 48%
→ GPT-5.2: 45%

None scored below 45%.

The most common issues:
→ SQL injection (still!)
→ Command injection
→ Insecure deserialization
→ Hardcoded credentials
→ Missing input validation

The AI models are getting better.
They're still not secure by default.

The training data included Stack Overflow circa 2015.
It shows.

AI-assisted development needs AI-assisted security review.
Or just... human review. By someone who knows what to look for.

-Nish

"Prompts are the new malware."

— CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report

In 2025, CrowdStrike tracked prompt injection attacks at 90+ organizations.

The injected prompts were used to:
→ Generate commands that stole credentials
→ Exfiltrate data through AI responses
→ Bypass content filters
→ Execute unauthorized actions

Prompt injection is the XSS of the AI era.

Malicious text hides inside trusted content.
When the AI processes it, that text becomes instructions.

March 2026: A backdoor in LiteLLM sat on PyPI for 3 hours.
47,000 downloads.

The package serves as the gateway for CrewAI, DSPy, Microsoft GraphRAG, and dozens of other AI agent frameworks.

If you're deploying AI systems, prompt injection testing is no longer optional.

LLM security assessment → zerosight360.com

We ran a phishing simulation last month.

Same company. Same employee list. Two campaigns.

Campaign A: Traditional phishing email.
→ 12% click rate

Campaign B: AI-generated phishing email.
→ 54% click rate

The AI email was perfect:
→ Correct tone for the industry
→ No grammar mistakes
→ Referenced real internal projects (scraped from LinkedIn)
→ Sent at optimal engagement time
→ Personalized per recipient

The old tells don't work anymore.

"Check for spelling errors" — AI doesn't make those.
"Does it look professional?" — Yes. Very.
"Is the sender suspicious?" — Spoofed perfectly.

The question isn't "does this look suspicious?"
It's "was I expecting this request?"

Security awareness training needs a complete rewrite.

-Nish

If you're deploying AI, here's the security checklist nobody gave you.

1. Model supply chain audit
→ Where did your model come from?
→ What was it trained on?
→ Who had access to the training pipeline?

2. Training data validation
→ Is it poisoned?
→ Is it licensed?
→ Does it contain PII?

3. Prompt injection testing
→ Can inputs manipulate outputs?
→ Can users escape their context?
→ What happens with adversarial inputs?

4. Output filtering & guardrails
→ What can the model say?
→ What actions can it take?
→ How do you prevent hallucinations from becoming actions?

5. Inference monitoring
→ What's being asked?
→ What's being answered?
→ Are there anomalies?

6. Model versioning & rollback
→ Can you revert quickly?
→ Are versions immutable?
→ Is there an audit trail?

AI/ML security assessment → zerosight360.com

Annual pentests. ✓
Quarterly audits. ✓
Monthly security training. ✓

Zero improvement in breach metrics.

Why?

Because we're measuring activity, not outcomes.

→ Pentest completed ≠ Findings remediated
→ Audit passed ≠ Actually secure
→ Training completed ≠ Behavior changed

The security industry sells comfort.
Compliance frameworks measure effort.
Neither measures actual risk reduction.

I've seen companies with perfect compliance scores get breached.
I've seen companies with "failing" audits that are actually secure.

The difference:
→ One optimizes for the auditor
→ One optimizes for the attacker

Which one are you building for?

-Nish

1.8 billion credentials were stolen in 2025.

Flashpoint tracked infostealers exfiltrating:
→ Over 1 billion email/password pairs
→ Browser cookies
→ Session tokens
→ Authentication certificates

276 million of those credentials included active session cookies.

That means: MFA bypass built-in.

The attacker doesn't need your password.
They don't need to beat your MFA.
They just replay your session.

Your identity is the new perimeter.
And it's under constant attack.

22% of breaches start with credential abuse.
97% of identity attacks are still password spray or brute-force.
389% YoY increase in account compromise incidents.

Credential theft at scale is industrialized.
Your defense needs to be too.

Identity security assessment → zerosight360.com

An intern found what 3 senior engineers missed.

Fresh eyes. No assumptions. Zero fear of asking "stupid" questions.

The vulnerability? A race condition in our authentication flow. It had been there for 18 months.

The senior engineers:
→ Knew the codebase too well
→ Assumed the auth module "just worked"
→ Focused on new features, not old code

The intern:
→ Read the code with fresh eyes
→ Asked "why does this work this way?"
→ Didn't assume anything was correct
→ Wasn't afraid to question senior decisions

Expertise is valuable.
Expertise is also blind spots.

The more you know about a system, the more you assume.
The more you assume, the more you miss.

Fresh perspectives aren't just nice to have.
They're security controls.

-Nish

Your response window is smaller than your average meeting.

29 minutes.

That's the average eCrime breakout time — the time from initial access to lateral movement.

The fastest? 14 minutes.

In 29 minutes, attackers can:
→ Establish persistence
→ Escalate privileges
→ Begin lateral movement
→ Start data exfiltration
→ Deploy ransomware

Your incident response plan probably assumes:
→ Someone notices the alert
→ They escalate to security
→ Security investigates
→ A call is scheduled
→ A decision is made

That takes longer than 29 minutes.

Incident response in 2026 isn't about processes.
It's about automation.

Detect → Contain → Investigate
All within the breakout window.

Incident response assessment → zerosight360.com

Why I stopped recommending annual pentests.

2020: 63 days from vulnerability disclosure to exploitation.
Annual testing could catch things in time.

2026: -7 days from disclosure to exploitation.
Exploits land before patches exist.

Annual pentests made sense when:
→ Attack windows were measured in months
→ Codebases changed slowly
→ Infrastructure was static
→ Compliance was the primary driver

None of those are true anymore.

Code changes daily.
Infrastructure changes hourly.
Attackers move in minutes.

Annual snapshots don't capture continuous risk.

The shift:
→ From annual to continuous
→ From point-in-time to always-on
→ From compliance checkbox to actual security

I still do pentests.
But they're part of continuous testing, not a replacement for it.

-Nish

The old advice is dead.

59% of compromised accounts had MFA enabled.

"Just turn on MFA" is no longer sufficient.

How attackers bypass MFA:

→ Session token theft
276M stolen credentials in 2025 included active session cookies.
No password needed. No MFA prompt. Just replay the session.

→ MFA fatigue
Flood the user with push notifications until they approve one.
Works more often than you'd think.

→ Real-time phishing
Proxy the auth flow. Capture the MFA code. Replay immediately.
Automated toolkits make this easy.

→ SIM swapping
Take over the phone number. Receive the SMS code.
Still works for SMS-based MFA.

MFA is still important.
MFA alone is not security.

Layered defense:
→ Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)
→ Session monitoring
→ Behavioral analytics
→ Device trust

Identity security assessment → zerosight360.com

The axios attack that could have been us.

March 31, 2026. Timeline:

→ 00:00 - Maintainer account compromised
→ 00:12 - Malicious code injected
→ 00:15 - Published to npm
→ 00:34 - 174,000 dependent packages affected
→ 03:00 - Discovered and removed

19 minutes to infect 140+ packages.
100 million weekly downloads affected.

Axios is in everything:
→ React apps
→ Node.js backends  
→ Mobile apps
→ Internal tools

Is axios in your dependency tree?
Probably.

Was your build pipeline pulling from npm during those 3 hours?
Maybe.

Do you have a way to know?

73% increase in malicious packages year-over-year.
454,600 new malicious packages in 2025 alone.

This isn't theoretical risk anymore.

-Nish

Security in 2027: What's coming.

Based on the data, here's what we're preparing for:

1. AI agents become attack vectors
Not just tools that help attackers — autonomous agents that ARE the attack. Agent-to-agent exploitation.

2. Identity replaces perimeter entirely
The last vestiges of network-based security fade. Everything is identity. Everywhere.

3. Supply chain attacks go nation-state
Coordinated, persistent, sophisticated. Not just opportunistic package hijacking.

4. Zero-day window hits -30 days
Exploitation campaigns will routinely begin weeks before public disclosure.

5. Compliance frameworks finally update
Regulations catch up to AI and continuous security. Annual attestations become monthly.

6. Security consolidation accelerates
Too many tools, not enough integration. Platforms win over point solutions.

7. Human-in-the-loop becomes mandatory
Fully automated security decisions prove too risky. Hybrid models emerge.

Some of this will age poorly. That's the point.

The future isn't predictable. Preparation is.

Strategic security planning → zerosight360.com

What 100 security assessments taught me.

After reviewing startups, enterprises, and everything in between:

→ Same 5 vulns in 80% of codebases
SQL injection. XSS. Broken auth. Insecure direct object references. Missing access controls. Still. In 2026.

→ Expensive tools, wrong configs
The tool isn't the problem. The deployment is. Default configs everywhere.

→ Compliance ≠ Security
I've seen SOC 2 certified companies with public S3 buckets. The auditor checks processes, not actual security.

→ The basics still win
Patching. MFA. Least privilege. Monitoring. Boring stuff done consistently beats fancy tools done poorly.

→ Shadow IT is everywhere
Every company has infrastructure they don't know about. Every. Single. One.

→ Developers want to do the right thing
They just don't always know what it is. Security education > security blame.

The work isn't glamorous.
But it works.

-Nish

241 days.

8 months of access.
8 months of data exfiltration.
8 months of lateral movement.
8 months of living in your network.

While you're:

→ Passing compliance audits

-Nish

"Buy our Zero Trust product."

Zero Trust is a framework, not a product you purchase.

The marketing version:
→ Buy this appliance
→ Deploy this agent
→ You now have Zero Trust

The reality:
→ Never trust, always verify
→ Assume breach
→ Verify explicitly
→ Use least privilege access
→ Micro-segmentation
→ Continuous validation

Zero Trust is architecture.
It's how you design systems, not what you buy.

It requires:
→ Identity as the control plane
→ Device trust verification
→ Network micro-segmentation
→ Application-level access controls
→ Continuous monitoring and validation

No single product gives you Zero Trust.
A vendor that claims otherwise is selling you a false sense of security.

Zero Trust architecture assessment → zerosight360.com
